query: Which material can be used for enhance glass-forming ability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor fraction of boron to a conventional metallic glass‐forming alloy will enhance its glass-forming ability by increasing atomic packing frustration.
generation.material_initial_state: A typical metallic glass precursor alloy (e.g., Zr–Cu–Ni–Al system) in its unmodified composition that exhibits limited glass formation under standard cooling conditions.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of approximately 2–5 atomic percent boron into the base alloy.
generation.conditions: Controlled rapid solidification conditions such as melt-spinning or copper mold casting to compare doped versus undoped samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron atoms, because of their small size and different bonding characteristics, are expected to disrupt local atomic order.
generation.mechanism: The atomic size mismatch and unique chemical interactions introduced by boron increase local packing frustration, thereby raising the nucleation barrier for crystals during cooling.
generation.predicted_outcome: A doped alloy will exhibit a higher amorphous phase fraction and an increased critical cooling rate for glass formation compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.baseline: The undoped alloy under identical processing conditions, which typically shows a lower fraction of the amorphous phase with a greater tendency to crystallize.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected primarily in metallic systems where atomic size mismatch can be exploited; the same intervention may not translate to nonmetallic glass systems.
generation.uncertainty: High, due to limited direct evidence and the variability of outcomes depending on the exact alloy composition and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples from the same base composition: one group with 0% boron (control) and one group with 2–5% boron added. Subject all samples to identical rapid solidification processes (e.g., melt-spinning) and analyze the structure.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to quantify the amorphous versus crystalline phase content
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine the crystallization onset temperature
Microstructural characterization (e.g., transmission electron microscopy) to assess atomic arrangements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not show a statistically significant increase in the amorphous phase fraction or an elevated crystallization onset temperature compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.
